query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy, applying a hybrid severe plastic deformation process—initial cryo-rolling to ~90% thickness reduction followed by warm-rolling at ~600 °C and a precisely controlled brief anneal (e.g., approximately 700 °C for 30–50 s, with optimization of the annealing parameters)—will induce the formation of refined nanocrystalline interfacial layers at the lamellar colony boundaries, thereby simultaneously enhancing yield strength and tensile ductility at room temperature relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies comprising CoCrFe-rich L12 and AlNi-rich B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a hybrid deformation route that begins with cryo-rolling to a true strain of approximately 2.4 (corresponding to ~90% thickness reduction) under an inert atmosphere, followed by warm-rolling at around 600 °C, and then a carefully optimized brief low-temperature anneal (e.g., near 700 °C for 30–50 seconds), with precise control of the annealing parameters to avoid over-recrystallization or coarsening.
generation.conditions: Processing should occur under an inert atmosphere with strain increments of ~1.2 per pass. Room-temperature tensile testing will be conducted to evaluate improvements in mechanical properties. Detailed process parameter optimization is required, particularly for the annealing stage, to ensure reliable formation of the nanocrystalline interfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention promotes the formation of a heterogeneous microstructure featuring refined nanocrystalline interfacial layers at the lamellar colony boundaries embedded within larger, coarse lamellae.
generation.mechanism: The high stored deformation energy from cryo-rolling drives shear-induced nanostructuring at the colony interfaces. Subsequent warm-rolling and a precisely controlled short anneal trigger localized partial recrystallization at the internal boundaries, resulting in refined nanocrystalline interlayers that are effective in deflecting or arresting microcrack propagation. Meanwhile, the coarser lamellae retain sufficient ductility and the ability to deform via twinning, thereby enhancing strain hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit an increase in yield strength by approximately 20–30% and an improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility by about 50%, along with a higher work-hardening rate that reduces microcrack nucleation at the internal boundaries.
generation.baseline: Unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEAs with conventional processing display a trade-off between strength and ductility, with a propensity for microcrack initiation at the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA processed under inert atmosphere and controlled deformation conditions. It is contingent on maintaining narrow process windows, especially for the annealing stage, to prevent over-recrystallization or coarsening that could nullify the beneficial effects on ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Precise outcomes depend on the fine-tuning of processing parameters—particularly the anneal time and temperature—as excessive recrystallization may degrade the nanocrystalline interfaces. Variability in processing conditions may also affect scalability and reproducibility, and further testing under different loading conditions is needed to fully assess the generality of the approach.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a set of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples using the proposed hybrid severe plastic deformation treatment with optimized and narrowly controlled annealing parameters. Compare their room-temperature tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure) and microstructural characteristics to those of unmodified control samples processed by conventional methods.
measurements: Tensile testing at room temperature to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation
Transmission and scanning electron microscopy (TEM, SEM) to characterize the formation and distribution of nanocrystalline interfacial layers
Kernel average misorientation (KAM) and other recrystallization indicators to assess microstructural heterogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the processed alloy does not show simultaneous improvement in both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of well-defined refined nanocrystalline interfacial layers (e.g., if over-recrystallization or coarsening dominates the interface structure).

cited_evidence.text: AbstractA lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was severely deformed by a novel hybrid-rolling process. During hybrid-rolling, the deformation was carried out in two stages, namely cryo-rolling followed by warm-rolling at 600 °C. The strain (ε) imparted in each of these steps was identical ~1.2, resulting in a total strain of ε~2.4 (corresponding to 90% reduction in thickness). The novel processing strategy resulted in an extremely heterogeneous microstructure consisting of retained lamellar and transformed nanocrystalline regions. Each of these regions consisted of different phases having different crystal structures and chemical compositions. The novel structure-composition dual heterogeneous microstructure originated from the stored energy of the cryo-rolling which accelerated transformations during subsequent low temperature warm-rolling. The dual heterogeneous microstructure yielded an unprecedented combination of strength (~2000 MPa) and ductility (~8%). The present study for the first time demonstrated that dual structure-composition heterogeneities can be a novel microstructural design strategy for achieving outstanding strength-ductility com

The origin of the NCRs can be related to the BLRs in the as-cast EHEA. BLRs are frequently reported in binary eutectics due to the instability in the lamellar growth. In the Stage I deformation by cryo-rolling, the imposed strain is partitioned more to the BLRs than the LRs due to their more open/relaxed structure. The larger strain partitioning is corroborated by the deformation induced disordering and nano-crystallization of the L12 in the BLRs. The higher stored energy of the BLRs provides the necessary driving force for the microstructural transformations during the subsequent warm-rolling (Stage II). The concomitant thermal energy and strain in Stage II deformation transforms the BLRs into NCRs. The NCRs show even further structural and chemical heterogeneities. The recrystallized regions are identified by lower KAM (volume fraction ~30%), while the deformed regions are evidenced by higher KAM and LAB network. The chemical heterogeneities are revealed by the presence of nanoscale phases with different compositions and crystal structures. This indicates that metastable microstructure of the as-cast EHEA breaks down during hybrid-rolling, accelerated and aided by the nanocrystal

It is interesting to note that monotonic cryo-rolling and novel variants such as hybrid-rolling (cryo- followed by warm-rolling) have been exploited by us in our earlier research to achieve novel structural and/or compositionally heterogeneous microstructure in multiphase lamellar eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA. The vastly different hardness of the constituent phases results in differential strain-partitioning, which in turn, results in differential stored energy or driving force for recrystallization during annealing and warm-rolling. In contrast, in the present research, the same cryo-rolling is exploited to tune the heterogeneous precipitation behavior for achieving the heterogeneous microstructure. These results clearly indicate significant opportunities for achieving novel heterogeneous microstructures in a wide range of HEAs through innovative processing by cryo-rolling.

proposals.intervention: Apply a hybrid severe plastic deformation procedure—namely, sequential cryo‐rolling (to a large strain of ~90% thickness reduction) followed by warm rolling at around 600 °C and a brief low-temperature anneal (e.g., 700 °C for 30–50 s)
proposals.conditions: Processing under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with room-temperature tensile testing for mechanical evaluation; strain increments of ~1.2 per pass during rolling
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of refined nanocrystalline interfacial layers at the lamellar colony boundaries embedded within the retained coarse lamellar microstructure
proposals.mechanism: The cryo-rolling stores high deformation energy that drives shear-induced nanostructuring at colony interfaces, while the subsequent warm rolling and short anneal promote partial recrystallization localized at the internal boundaries. This produces highly heterogeneous interfacial zones capable of deflecting or arresting microcrack propagation. At the same time, the coarser lamellae retain sufficient ductility and allow for twin formation, thus boosting strain hardening and delaying catastrophic failure.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit simultaneously enhanced yield strength (an increase of ~20–30%) and improved room-temperature tensile ductility (increased elongation by ~50%), with a higher work-hardening rate that reduces microcrack nucleation at internal boundaries.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single intervention directly targets the weakness of dual-phase lamellar colonies—the propensity for microcrack initiation at internal boundaries—by engineering those boundaries to be more resistant to crack propagation. Simultaneously, the overall heterogeneous microstructure yields higher strength while preserving (or even enhancing) ductility, thereby overcoming the conventional trade-off between these properties.

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention directly targets the microcrack initiation at the internal boundaries of the dual-phase lamellar colonies by deliberately engineering those interfaces into refined, nanocrystalline layers, which is exactly the root cause of the room‐temperature brittleness in these alloys.
critiques.constraints: The proposed method adheres to the constraints by working on the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy, maintaining the dual-phase lamellar structure, employing processing conditions (inert atmosphere, specific strain increments) that are in line with previous work, and aiming to improve both strength and tensile ductility simultaneously.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound. The severe plastic deformation through cryo-rolling generates high stored deformation energy that can induce shear-driven nanostructuring at colony interfaces, while the subsequent warm rolling and brief low-temperature anneal partially recrystallize the interfaces. This hybrid route modifies the boundaries to deflect or arrest microcrack propagation without compromising the bulk ductile behavior of the coarser lamellae.
critiques.feasibility: The processing steps (cryo-rolling, warm rolling, and short-duration annealing) are all well established in metal processing. As supported by several publications (e.g., records PMC6687781 and PMC7142141), such hybrid severe plastic deformation routes are experimentally feasible with available methods.
critiques.evidence: The provided evidence from multiple literature records, particularly the work in PMC6687781 and PMC7142141, supports the use of a hybrid-rolling process in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to attain dual heterogeneous microstructures leading to simultaneously enhanced strength and ductility.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk lies in the sensitivity of the processing parameters. Inadequate control during the warm rolling or the subsequent low-temperature anneal could result in over-recrystallization or coarsening, potentially degrading the intended nanocrystalline interfaces and thus adverse effects on ductility.
critiques.fix: Implement detailed process parameter optimization studies—in particular, narrow the annealing time and temperature window—to ensure that the nanocrystalline interfaces are consistently produced without over-recrystallization or coarsening.

decision.rationale: Candidate direction A directly targets the key weakness of the dual-phase lamellar colonies by engineering the internal boundaries to form refined nanocrystalline layers that can deflect crack propagation. The provided evidence and critiques substantiate the physical soundness and feasibility of applying a hybrid severe plastic deformation process (cryo-rolling followed by warm rolling and a brief low-temperature anneal) to achieve a dual heterogeneous microstructure with superior strength and ductility. The critic’s fix—narrowing the annealing time and temperature window to avoid over-recrystallization or coarsening—is reasonable and can be implemented via process parameter optimization.
